title: Passenger Transport
summary: Bus inspections, loading and baggage, hazmat limits, rider supervision, safe driving at crossings and curves, and practices a bus driver must avoid.

blocks.text: You need a CDL with a passenger (P) endorsement to drive a vehicle designed to carry 16 or more people, including the driver.

items: Pass a knowledge test on Sections 2 (driving safely) and 4 (transporting passengers) of the CDL manual.
If your bus has air brakes, also pass the air brakes test (Section 5).
Pass the skills tests for the class of vehicle you drive.

The endorsement applies to buses in any class (A, B or C). A CLP with a P endorsement carries a P restriction: no passengers other than examiners, inspectors, other trainees and the accompanying CDL holder.

blocks.text: Review the previous driver's inspection report. Sign it only if the defects reported earlier have been certified as repaired or as not needing repair. Your signature certifies that.

items: Make sure these work before driving: service brakes (including air hose couplings if you pull a trailer), parking brake, steering, lights and reflectors, horn, wipers, mirrors, coupling devices, wheels, rims, tires and emergency equipment.
Front wheels must not have recapped or regrooved tires.
Carry a fire extinguisher and emergency reflectors: 3 reflective triangles, or at least 6 fuses, or 3 liquid-burning flares.
Carry spare electrical fuses unless the bus has circuit breakers.
Close any open emergency exits and access panels (baggage, restroom service, engine) before driving.

blocks.text: Always check the interior, because people sometimes damage buses left unattended.

items: Aisles and stairwells always clear.
Handholds, railings, floor covering and emergency exit handles in good shape.
Signaling devices working, including the restroom emergency buzzer if there is a restroom.
All seats safe and securely fastened to the bus.
The Emergency Exit sign clearly visible. A red emergency door light, if present, must work and be on at night or whenever your outside lights are on.
You may lock some roof hatches partly open for fresh air, but not as a regular habit. Remember the bus now needs more overhead clearance.
Always wear the driver's seat belt.

blocks.text: Never drive with an emergency exit door or window open.

items: Do not let riders leave carry-on baggage in a doorway or aisle; nothing should be there to trip anyone.
Secure baggage and freight so the driver can move freely, riders can exit by any door or window in an emergency, and falling or shifting carry-ons cannot injure riders.

blocks.text: Most hazardous materials cannot go on a bus. Shippers must mark hazmat containers with the material's name, ID number and hazard label. There are nine different four-inch, diamond-shaped hazard labels. If you are not sure the rules allow an item, do not carry it.

rows: Small-arms ammunition labeled ORM-D, emergency hospital supplies, and drugs. Small amounts of some other hazmat if the shipper cannot send it any other way.
Division 2.3 poison gas, liquid Class 6 poison, tear gas, irritating material.
Not in the space occupied by people, except small-arms ammunition.
Not in the space occupied by people.
No more than 500 pounds of allowed hazmat in all, and no more than 100 pounds of any one class.

items: Riders sometimes bring unlabeled hazmat. Do not let them carry on common hazards such as car batteries or gasoline.
In the manual's hazard table, hair spray and charcoal are listed as ORM-D; fuel oil and lighter fluid are combustible liquids.

blocks.text: No rider may stand forward of the rear of the driver's seat. Buses built for standing riders mark this with a two-inch line on the floor (or another method), called the standee line. All standing riders stay behind it.

items: Explain rules about smoking, drinking or radio use at the start of the trip to avoid trouble later.
Scan the inside of the bus as well as the road ahead, sides and rear. You may need to remind riders to keep arms and heads inside.
At destinations and intermediate stops, announce the location, the reason for stopping, the next departure time and the bus number.
Remind riders to take their carry-ons. If the aisle is lower than the seats, warn them about the step-down before you come to a complete stop.
Charter drivers should not let riders board until departure time, to help prevent theft or vandalism.
Riders can stumble getting on or off and when the bus starts or stops. Caution them to watch their step, wait for them to sit down or brace themselves before starting, and start and stop smoothly.

Do not put a drunk or disruptive rider off where it is unsafe for them. The next scheduled stop or a well-lit area with other people may be safer. Follow your carrier's guidelines for disruptive riders.
Bus crashes often happen at intersections. Be careful even when a signal or stop sign controls other traffic.

Pulling out of a stop, buses sometimes scrape mirrors or hit passing vehicles. Remember your clearance, watch for poles and tree limbs, and wait for a gap big enough to accelerate and merge. Never assume others will brake for you.

Crashes on curves usually come from too much speed, often when rain or snow has made the road slippery. The posted speed on a banked curve is safe for cars in good weather but may be too fast for many buses. With good traction a speeding bus may roll over; with poor traction it may slide off. If the bus leans toward the outside, you are going too fast.
Stop between 15 and 50 feet before a railroad crossing.
Look and listen both ways. Open the forward door if it helps you see or hear a train.
After a train passes, make sure no other train is coming on another track.
With a manual transmission, never change gears while crossing the tracks.

blocks.caption: An EXEMPT plaque under the crossbuck: a bus need not stop, but must still slow down and check carefully.

rows: No stop needed, but slow down and check
Streetcar crossings; where a police officer or flagman directs traffic; a green traffic signal; crossings marked exempt or abandoned.
Drawbridge with no signal or attendant
Stop at least 50 feet before the draw and make sure it is completely closed.
Drawbridge with a green light or attendant
No stop needed, but slow down and make sure it is safe.

sections.heading: After the trip and prohibited practices

items: Inspect your bus at the end of each shift.
Interstate carrier drivers must complete a written report for each bus driven, listing any defect that would affect safety or cause a breakdown. If there are none, the report says so.
Report rider damage to handholds, seats, emergency exits and windows so it can be fixed.
Mass transit drivers also check passenger signaling devices and brake-door interlocks.

blocks.text: Avoid fueling with riders aboard unless absolutely necessary, and never refuel in a closed building with riders aboard. Do not talk with riders or do anything distracting while driving. Do not tow or push a disabled bus with riders aboard unless getting off would be unsafe, and then only to the nearest safe spot.

A transit coach brake-door interlock applies the brakes and holds the throttle at idle while the rear door is open. It releases when you close the rear door. Do not use it in place of the parking brake.

keyPoints: A passenger endorsement is needed for vehicles designed for 16 or more people, including the driver; add the air brakes test if equipped.
Sign the previous driver's report only if earlier defects were certified repaired or not needing repair.
No recapped or regrooved front tires; carry 3 triangles (or 6 fuses or 3 flares), an extinguisher, and spare fuses unless you have circuit breakers.
Never carry Division 2.3 poison gas, liquid Class 6 poison or tear gas; limit allowed hazmat to 500 lbs total and 100 lbs per class.
No rider may stand forward of the rear of the driver's seat (the standee line).
Stop 15-50 feet before railroad crossings and never shift gears on the tracks; stop 50 feet before an unattended drawbridge.
Never refuel in a closed building with riders aboard, and never use the brake-door interlock as a parking brake.
